course.title: Pandas Mastery
course.subtitle: Complete Data Analysis Program
course.tagline: Learn Data. Understand Data. Analyse Data. Think like a Data Analyst.
course.description: Pandas from the first Series to groupby, merges, time series and a machine-learning hand-off. Twenty modules, ten learning sections each, every code sample executed before it ships, and examples that use BroCode's own data shapes: courses, lessons, quiz attempts and progress.
prerequisites: An idea of what a table is — rows and columns
outcomes: Create, inspect and select from Series and DataFrame objects
Filter rows with loc, iloc, Boolean masks and query
Convert dtypes deliberately and handle missing values with a reason
Clean duplicates, text, categories and outliers into a validated table
Read and write CSV, JSON, SQL and Parquet without losing types
Merge and concatenate datasets and prove the join did not fan out
Group, aggregate and reshape data into the table a question needs
Work with datetimes, resampling and rolling windows
Profile memory and process files larger than RAM in chunks
Prepare a leakage-free dataset for scikit-learn
Run a full EDA and explain the findings as a data analyst

modules.title: Pandas Foundations
modules.goal: Understand what Pandas is for, what a DataFrame is, and how it differs from a list, a NumPy array, Excel and SQL.

topics.title: What a DataFrame gives you
topics.body: A DataFrame is a table with named columns of different types. `shape` reports rows and columns; a column is a Series, so statistics are one method away.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

students = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Aman", "Riya", "Rahul"], "marks": [85, 92, 78]})
print(students.shape)
print(students["marks"].mean())

topics.title: A Series is one labelled column
topics.body: A Series pairs values with an index. Give it string labels and `.loc` reads by label instead of by position.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

marks = pd.Series([85, 92, 78], index=["Aman", "Riya", "Rahul"])
print(marks.loc["Riya"])
print(marks.max())

topics.title: Build a DataFrame from a dict
topics.body: Each dict key becomes a column and the values become its rows. This is the shape every CSV becomes after `read_csv`.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [120, 90]})
print(df.columns.tolist())
print(df["sales"].sum())

topics.title: Every DataFrame has an index
topics.body: Rows carry labels too. The default index is 0, 1, 2, and `.loc[1]` means the row labelled 1 — not the second row after a sort.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"sales": [120, 90, 60]})
print(df.index.tolist())
print(df.loc[1, "sales"])

topics.title: Lists concatenate, Series add
topics.body: `+` on two Python lists joins them; on two Series it adds element by element. That difference is the whole reason Pandas exists.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

print([1, 2] + [3, 4])
print((pd.Series([1, 2]) + pd.Series([3, 4])).tolist())

topics.title: Rows, columns and records
topics.body: A row is one record and a column is one field across records. `len(df)` counts records, `df.columns` lists fields, and the two numbers answer different questions.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "city": ["Pune", "Delhi", "Pune"]})
print(len(df), len(df.columns))
print(df["city"].nunique())

topics.title: Structured data has a schema
topics.body: A structured table has the same fields on every row with a type per field. Scraped text or a JSON blob is unstructured: it needs parsing before it can be counted.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

rows = [{"id": 1, "tags": "a"}, {"id": 2}]
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(df.notna().all(axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: Pandas, Excel and SQL in one line
topics.body: Excel is a manual grid, SQL queries a database in place, Pandas runs code over data in memory. The same three operations — select, filter, group — exist in all of them.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
print(df[df["sales"] > 5].groupby("city")["sales"].sum().to_dict())

topics.title: pd is only an alias
topics.body: `import pandas as pd` binds the module to a short name; `pd` is a convention, not a requirement. Code that imports `pandas` keeps working but reads like everyone else's code does not.
topics.code:
import pandas as pandas_lib

df = pandas_lib.DataFrame({"a": [1]})
print(type(df).__name__)

interviewBank.q: Why does Pandas exist when Python already has lists and NumPy has arrays?
interviewBank.answer: Lists and NumPy arrays are positional: column 0 means nothing. Pandas adds labelled rows and columns of mixed types, alignment by label, missing-value handling and grouping, which are the operations tabular analysis actually needs. NumPy is still underneath for the fast numeric path.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a Series and a DataFrame?
interviewBank.answer: A Series is one labelled, typed 1-D array — one column plus its index. A DataFrame is a dict-like collection of Series that share one index, so it is 2-D with named columns. `df["col"]` returns a Series; `df[["col"]]` returns a one-column DataFrame.

interviewBank.q: What is a DataFrame internally, in one sentence?
interviewBank.answer: A dict-like collection of Series that share one index, with a column axis that carries names and dtypes. That is why selecting a column returns a Series and aligning two frames matches rows by label.

interviewBank.q: When would a plain Python dict be enough instead of a DataFrame?
interviewBank.answer: When the data is a single record, there are no repeated rows to aggregate, and no alignment or missing-value handling is needed. A one-row lookup is a dict; a table of many rows with grouping is a frame.

defenseBank.q: A teammate says "use Pandas, it is faster than Python loops". How do you answer precisely?
defenseBank.answer: Pandas is faster for column-wise work because operations run in compiled code over contiguous blocks. It is not faster automatically: `apply(axis=1)` and `iterrows` still run Python per row and can be slower than a plain loop. The speed comes from vectorised column operations, not from the word Pandas.
steps: Name the vectorised call that replaces the loop.
Say when a loop is still the right tool.

defenseBank.q: When would you choose Excel or SQL over Pandas?
defenseBank.answer: Excel when a non-programmer has to edit and review the sheet. SQL when the data already lives in a database and is too large to pull into memory. Pandas wins when the analysis needs code, reproducibility and joins across files.
steps: State who has to read the result.
State where the data lives and how big it is.
Name the reproducibility cost of the alternative.

topics.body: `reindex` lines the object up with the labels you name: existing ones keep their value, missing ones become NaN. It is the alignment tool.

topics.body: Row-wise input has no names, so `columns=` supplies them. Without it the columns are 0, 1, 2 and every later selection is positional.

interviewBank.q: What does index alignment mean, and where does it surprise people?
interviewBank.answer: When two pandas objects combine, rows are matched by index label rather than position. A filtered Series keeps its original labels, so adding it back to the full frame leaves NaN on the removed rows. Sorting or resetting the index first is the usual fix.

interviewBank.q: Why is `df['col']` sometimes a Series and sometimes a DataFrame?
interviewBank.answer: A single label returns the column as a Series; a list of labels returns a DataFrame with those columns. The bracket count is the type switch, which matters because `to_csv` and plotting helpers expect a frame.

interviewBank.q: Why must an index be unique before a join?
interviewBank.answer: A join matches labels, so a duplicate label on either side multiplies the matched rows into a fan-out. Convert to a key column and deduplicate before merging, or use `validate` so the duplicate fails loudly.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `set_index` and `reset_index`?
interviewBank.answer: `set_index` demotes a column into the row labels; `reset_index` promotes the labels back into a column and restores 0..n. They are inverses, and a round trip loses a meaningful index only if you choose to.

defenseBank.q: Justify keeping a meaningful index instead of resetting to 0..n.
defenseBank.answer: A meaningful index makes label lookups and alignment explicit, and it keeps `merge` on the index cheap. Reset it when the label has no meaning or repeats — a duplicate index makes `.loc` return several rows and silently inflates joins.

defenseBank.q: A learner's table has 3 columns and 1,000 rows, and `df.sum()` returns one number per column. Explain the rule.
defenseBank.answer: Reduction defaults to `axis=0`, so it collapses the row axis and leaves one value per column. `df.sum(axis=1)` collapses the columns instead and returns one total per row.

defense.q: Justify keeping a meaningful index instead of resetting to 0..n.
defense.answer: A meaningful index makes label lookups and alignment explicit, and it keeps `merge` on the index cheap. Reset it when the label has no meaning or repeats — a duplicate index makes `.loc` return several rows and silently inflates joins.

defense.q: A learner's table has 3 columns and 1,000 rows, and `df.sum()` returns one number per column. Explain the rule.
defense.answer: Reduction defaults to `axis=0`, so it collapses the row axis and leaves one value per column. `df.sum(axis=1)` collapses the columns instead and returns one total per row.

modules.title: Inspecting Data
modules.goal: Profile a table in one pass: shape, dtypes, missing counts, distinct values and distribution.

topics.title: head and tail show the edges
topics.body: `head(2)` and `tail(2)` preview the first and last rows without loading anything extra, which is the first thing to run on an unknown file.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3, 4], "marks": [80, 90, 70, 60]})
print(df.head(2)["id"].tolist())
print(df.tail(2)["id"].tolist())

topics.title: shape, size and ndim
topics.body: `shape` is (rows, columns), `size` is rows × columns, `ndim` is 2 for every DataFrame. Printing all three catches a wrong separator immediately.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
print(df.shape, df.size, df.ndim)

topics.title: dtypes are the contract
topics.body: A numeric column stored as text breaks every mean. `dtypes` shows the truth, and `object` or `str` on a number column is the warning sign.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "name": ["a", "b"], "fee": [10.5, 20.0]})
print(df.dtypes.astype(str).tolist())

topics.title: describe summarises every numeric column
topics.body: `describe()` returns count, mean, std, min, quartiles and max in one call. Comparing mean and median there is the fastest skew check.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"marks": [10, 20, 30, 40]})
print(df["marks"].describe().round(1).tolist())

topics.title: value_counts answers what is in a column
topics.body: `value_counts` counts each distinct value, sorted by frequency. `nunique` gives just the number of distinct values.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"]})
print(df["city"].value_counts().to_dict())
print(df["city"].nunique())

topics.title: sample shows rows you did not look at
topics.body: `head` and `tail` only show the edges. `sample(n, random_state=...)` draws from anywhere in the table, which is how a suspicious middle row is found.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": range(10)})
print(df.sample(2, random_state=1)["id"].tolist())

topics.title: select_dtypes picks by type
topics.body: `select_dtypes` returns only the columns of the types you name, so scaling, dates and text can be handled by separate pipelines.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [1.5], "c": ["x"]})
print(df.select_dtypes("number").columns.tolist())

topics.title: empty answers a different question than zero rows
topics.body: `empty` is True when there are no elements at all — no rows OR no columns. A frame with rows and zero columns is empty too, which catches a wrong `usecols`.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

print(pd.DataFrame().empty)
print(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1]}).empty)

topics.title: count ignores missing, size does not
topics.body: `count` returns non-missing values per column; `size` returns rows × columns. Comparing them shows how much of a column is actually usable.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3]})
print(df["a"].count(), df["a"].size)

interviewBank.q: You open a CSV and every column is `object`. What do you check first?
interviewBank.answer: Whether the file parsed at all: a wrong separator, a header row inside the data or thousands separators turn numbers into text. `df.head()` plus `df.dtypes` tells you which, then re-read with the right `sep`, `thousands` or `dtype`.

interviewBank.q: What does `describe()` hide that a histogram would not?
interviewBank.answer: Shape. Mean, std and quartiles can be identical for a bimodal column and a normal one, and they say nothing about gaps, spikes or a hard cap. Plot or bin the column before trusting the summary.

interviewBank.q: Why sample instead of only looking at head?
interviewBank.answer: Sorted or grouped exports put the anomalies in the middle: a bad batch, a blank block, a wrong unit. A seeded sample reaches rows head and tail never show, and the seed keeps the review reproducible.

interviewBank.q: What does a clean `describe()` still hide?
interviewBank.answer: Shape. Identical mean, std and quartiles can describe a normal column and a bimodal one. Bin or plot the column before drawing a conclusion from the summary.

defenseBank.q: Argue for profiling a dataset before writing any cleaning code.
defenseBank.answer: Cleaning decisions depend on facts the profile supplies: which columns are text, where missing values sit, whether a category is consistent. Cleaning first means guessing, and a guess like filling a numeric gap with 0 can be wrong for the domain.
steps: Name the facts a profile returns.
Name one decision each fact changes.

defenseBank.q: When is `value_counts` the wrong tool?
defenseBank.answer: On a high-cardinality column such as an id or a free-text field: nearly every value is unique, so the table is long and uninformative. Use `nunique`, a head/tail of the counts, or bin the column first.
steps: Say what the output looks like.

learn.title: head and tail show the edges
learn.body: `head(2)` and `tail(2)` preview the first and last rows without loading anything extra, which is the first thing to run on an unknown file.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3, 4], "marks": [80, 90, 70, 60]})
print(df.head(2)["id"].tolist())
print(df.tail(2)["id"].tolist())

learn.title: shape, size and ndim
learn.body: `shape` is (rows, columns), `size` is rows × columns, `ndim` is 2 for every DataFrame. Printing all three catches a wrong separator immediately.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
print(df.shape, df.size, df.ndim)

learn.title: dtypes are the contract
learn.body: A numeric column stored as text breaks every mean. `dtypes` shows the truth, and `object` or `str` on a number column is the warning sign.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "name": ["a", "b"], "fee": [10.5, 20.0]})
print(df.dtypes.astype(str).tolist())

learn.title: describe summarises every numeric column
learn.body: `describe()` returns count, mean, std, min, quartiles and max in one call. Comparing mean and median there is the fastest skew check.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"marks": [10, 20, 30, 40]})
print(df["marks"].describe().round(1).tolist())

learn.title: value_counts answers what is in a column
learn.body: `value_counts` counts each distinct value, sorted by frequency. `nunique` gives just the number of distinct values.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"]})
print(df["city"].value_counts().to_dict())
print(df["city"].nunique())

learn.title: sample shows rows you did not look at
learn.body: `head` and `tail` only show the edges. `sample(n, random_state=...)` draws from anywhere in the table, which is how a suspicious middle row is found.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": range(10)})
print(df.sample(2, random_state=1)["id"].tolist())

learn.title: select_dtypes picks by type
learn.body: `select_dtypes` returns only the columns of the types you name, so scaling, dates and text can be handled by separate pipelines.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [1.5], "c": ["x"]})
print(df.select_dtypes("number").columns.tolist())

learn.title: empty answers a different question than zero rows
learn.body: `empty` is True when there are no elements at all — no rows OR no columns. A frame with rows and zero columns is empty too, which catches a wrong `usecols`.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

print(pd.DataFrame().empty)
print(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1]}).empty)

learn.title: count ignores missing, size does not
learn.body: `count` returns non-missing values per column; `size` returns rows × columns. Comparing them shows how much of a column is actually usable.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3]})
print(df["a"].count(), df["a"].size)

interview.q: You open a CSV and every column is `object`. What do you check first?
interview.answer: Whether the file parsed at all: a wrong separator, a header row inside the data or thousands separators turn numbers into text. `df.head()` plus `df.dtypes` tells you which, then re-read with the right `sep`, `thousands` or `dtype`.

interview.q: What does `describe()` hide that a histogram would not?
interview.answer: Shape. Mean, std and quartiles can be identical for a bimodal column and a normal one, and they say nothing about gaps, spikes or a hard cap. Plot or bin the column before trusting the summary.

interview.q: Why sample instead of only looking at head?
interview.answer: Sorted or grouped exports put the anomalies in the middle: a bad batch, a blank block, a wrong unit. A seeded sample reaches rows head and tail never show, and the seed keeps the review reproducible.

interview.q: What does a clean `describe()` still hide?
interview.answer: Shape. Identical mean, std and quartiles can describe a normal column and a bimodal one. Bin or plot the column before drawing a conclusion from the summary.

topics.title: loc selects by label
topics.body: `df.loc[row_label, column_label]` always means labels, and slices include the stop label — the opposite of a Python list slice.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"marks": [85, 92, 78]}, index=["a", "b", "c"])
print(df.loc["b", "marks"])
print(df.loc["a":"b", "marks"].tolist())

topics.title: iloc selects by position
topics.body: `df.iloc[0, 1]` is first row, second column. Slices exclude the stop, like Python. Use it when there is no meaningful label.
topics.code:

print(df.iloc[0, 1])

topics.title: A Boolean mask keeps the True rows
topics.body: A comparison returns a same-shape mask; putting it inside the brackets filters the rows. The result keeps the original index labels.
topics.code:

topics.title: query reads like a condition
topics.body: `query` takes a string, so `and`/`or` work and the condition can come from a config value. Column names with spaces need backticks.
topics.code:

topics.title: isin and between test a range or a set
topics.body: `isin` answers "is this value in my list", `between` answers "is it inside this interval". Both return masks that combine with `&`.
topics.code:

topics.title: at and iat read one cell fast
topics.body: `at` is a label lookup and `iat` is a positional one, both for a single scalar. They are the cheapest read when you know exactly which cell you need.
topics.code:

topics.title: where keeps the shape, mask keeps the shape
topics.body: `where` keeps a value where the condition is True and replaces the rest; `mask` does the opposite. Both return the original shape, unlike filtering.
topics.code:

topics.title: filter matches column names, not rows
topics.body: `filter(like=...)` selects columns by their name pattern. It is not a row filter; rows belong to a Boolean mask or `query`.

topics.title: A mask combines with & only inside brackets
topics.body: `&` binds tighter than `>` in Python, so every comparison needs its own parentheses; `and` on an array raises because it wants one truth value.

interviewBank.q: What is the practical difference between loc and iloc?
interviewBank.answer: loc uses labels and includes the stop of a slice; iloc uses 0-based positions and excludes it. The trap is that a default RangeIndex makes them look identical until a filter or sort reorders the labels.

interviewBank.q: Why is chained assignment risky, and what replaces it?
interviewBank.answer: `df[df.a > 1]["b"] = 0` may write into a temporary copy, so the original frame never changes. The supported form is one `.loc` call: `df.loc[df.a > 1, "b"] = 0`, which writes into the frame itself.

interviewBank.q: When is `where` the right tool instead of a Boolean filter?
interviewBank.answer: When the row count and index must stay intact — capping outliers, blanking invalid cells, or building two aligned branches. Filtering removes rows, so anything that must line up with the original frame needs `where` or `mask`.

interviewBank.q: Why can a filter return an empty frame without any error?
interviewBank.answer: Filtering is a comparison, and a comparison that matches nothing is perfectly valid. The cause is almost always dtype (text compared to a number), case or whitespace in a category, or a column name that silently differs.

defenseBank.q: A query returns 0 rows and no error. Walk through how you would debug it.
defenseBank.answer: Check the dtype being compared (text "85" never exceeds 80), check for whitespace or case in a string category, print the mask's sum to see if it is all False, and confirm the column name exists with `df.columns`. A silent empty frame is always a comparison that never matched.
steps: Print dtype and a sample value.

defenseBank.q: Explain why filtering keeps the old index, and when you would reset it.
defenseBank.answer: Filtering selects rows, so their labels travel with them; the gaps are information that the row came from position 7. Reset when the index is about to be used positionally, exported, or merged, because duplicate or gapped labels confuse `.loc`.
steps: Say what the label means after filtering.

modules.title: Data Types and Conversion
modules.goal: Read a dtype, choose the right one, and convert without turning bad values into silent garbage.

topics.title: astype changes the stored type
topics.body: `astype` converts between compatible types and raises on values it cannot represent. It is the explicit way to make an integer column a float.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])
print(s.dtype)
print(s.astype(float).dtype)

topics.title: to_numeric can coerce bad values
topics.body: `pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce")` turns unparseable entries into NaN instead of raising, which is how a dirty price column becomes usable.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.Series(["10", "x", "30"])
clean = pd.to_numeric(raw, errors="coerce")
print(clean.isna().sum())
print(clean.fillna(0).tolist())

topics.title: to_datetime parses dates once
topics.body: Parsing at load time makes `.dt` available and turns comparisons into date comparisons. `errors="coerce"` puts invalid dates into NaT.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(["2026-01-05", "2026-02-10"]))
print(dates.dt.month.tolist())
print((dates.dt.dayofweek < 5).tolist())

topics.title: convert_dtypes picks nullable types
topics.body: `convert_dtypes` chooses the nullable extension types, so an integer column with a gap becomes `Int64` instead of silently turning into floats.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, None, 3])
print(s.dtype)
print(s.convert_dtypes().dtype)

topics.title: category pays off on repeats
topics.body: A category stores each distinct string once plus integer codes. Memory drops sharply when a column repeats a few values across many rows.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

text = pd.Series(["pune", "delhi"] * 500)
packed = text.astype("category")
print(packed.dtype)
print(packed.cat.categories.tolist())

topics.title: Nullable Int64 keeps integers and gaps
topics.body: The classic `int64` cannot hold NaN, so a gap forces float. The nullable `Int64` extension stores `pd.NA` and keeps the integer arithmetic.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, None], dtype="Int64")
print(s.dtype)
print(s.sum())

topics.title: A category dtype can be ordered
topics.body: Declaring the categories and `ordered=True` lets comparisons and sorting follow the domain order, which is what turns a status column into a sortable one.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["medium", "low"], dtype=pd.CategoricalDtype(["low", "medium", "high"], ordered=True))
print((s == "low").tolist())
print(s.cat.categories.tolist())

topics.title: to_datetime fixes the unit
topics.body: Passing `format=` or `unit=` makes parsing explicit. Without it pandas guesses, and two files in one pipeline can guess differently.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(["05/01/2026"]), format="%d/%m/%Y")
print(s.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist())

topics.title: astype on one column only
topics.body: A per-column conversion keeps the rest of the frame untouched: build a dict or use `astype` on the Series, so a numeric column does not turn the whole frame into text.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["1", "2"], "name": ["a", "b"]})
df["id"] = df["id"].astype(int)
print(df.dtypes.astype(str).tolist())

interviewBank.q: Why does an integer column with one missing value become float?
interviewBank.answer: The classic int64 dtype has no NaN representation, so pandas promotes the column to float64 to hold the gap. The nullable `Int64` extension dtype keeps integers and stores missing as `pd.NA`, which is what `convert_dtypes` selects.

interviewBank.q: When does `category` hurt instead of help?
interviewBank.answer: When the column is nearly unique: codes plus a large category array cost more than object pointers. It also complicates operations that need arbitrary values, and adding a new category has to update the dtype. It wins with a small, repeated vocabulary.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer an explicit dtype map over inference at load?
interviewBank.answer: Inference changes with the data: one blank cell turns an integer column into float, and a join key that was numeric stops matching. An explicit map fails at the boundary, where the cause is obvious, instead of at the join.

interviewBank.q: When is `object` dtype a real problem?
interviewBank.answer: When the column holds numbers or repeated text: arithmetic either fails or falls back to Python, memory grows with pointer overhead, and grouping is slower. It is fine for genuinely heterogeneous values, which usually means the column should be split.

defenseBank.q: Argue for converting dtypes at load time rather than after cleaning.
defenseBank.answer: Typed data fails loudly and cheaply: `parse_dates` or `dtype=` makes a wrong file fail at the boundary instead of at the groupby. It also avoids the float promotion trap and keeps memory predictable from the first line.

defenseBank.q: An analyst says "just use errors='coerce' everywhere". What is the risk?
defenseBank.answer: Coercion hides the cause: a wrongly specified decimal separator turns every value into NaN and the analysis reports zero without an error. Coerce, then count and inspect the NaNs it created before continuing.

interview.q: Why does an integer column with one missing value become float?
interview.answer: The classic int64 dtype has no NaN representation, so pandas promotes the column to float64 to hold the gap. The nullable `Int64` extension dtype keeps integers and stores missing as `pd.NA`, which is what `convert_dtypes` selects.

interview.q: When does `category` hurt instead of help?
interview.answer: When the column is nearly unique: codes plus a large category array cost more than object pointers. It also complicates operations that need arbitrary values, and adding a new category has to update the dtype. It wins with a small, repeated vocabulary.

interview.q: Why prefer an explicit dtype map over inference at load?
interview.answer: Inference changes with the data: one blank cell turns an integer column into float, and a join key that was numeric stops matching. An explicit map fails at the boundary, where the cause is obvious, instead of at the join.

interview.q: When is `object` dtype a real problem?
interview.answer: When the column holds numbers or repeated text: arithmetic either fails or falls back to Python, memory grows with pointer overhead, and grouping is slower. It is fine for genuinely heterogeneous values, which usually means the column should be split.

defense.q: Argue for converting dtypes at load time rather than after cleaning.
defense.answer: Typed data fails loudly and cheaply: `parse_dates` or `dtype=` makes a wrong file fail at the boundary instead of at the groupby. It also avoids the float promotion trap and keeps memory predictable from the first line.

defense.q: An analyst says "just use errors='coerce' everywhere". What is the risk?
defense.answer: Coercion hides the cause: a wrongly specified decimal separator turns every value into NaN and the analysis reports zero without an error. Coerce, then count and inspect the NaNs it created before continuing.

modules.title: Arithmetic and Vectorized Operations
modules.goal: Compute new columns with column arithmetic instead of loops, and know when apply is the honest choice.

topics.title: Column arithmetic creates a column
topics.body: Two Series of the same length combine element by element, and assigning the result adds a column. No loop, no index bookkeeping.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"price": [100, 200], "qty": [2, 3]})
df["total"] = df["price"] * df["qty"]
print(df["total"].tolist())

topics.title: assign keeps the chain readable
topics.body: `assign` returns a new frame with the column added, so a pipeline can stay one expression and the original frame is untouched.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"marks": [40, 80]})
out = df.assign(passed=df["marks"] >= 50)
print(out["passed"].tolist())
print("passed" in df.columns)

topics.title: clip keeps values inside a range
topics.body: `clip(lower, upper)` pins out-of-range values without an if. It is the standard guard before a ratio, a score or a pixel write.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([-5, 50, 150])
print(s.clip(0, 100).tolist())

topics.title: map translates values with a dict
topics.body: `map` looks each value up in a dict, which is how codes become labels. A value missing from the dict becomes NaN.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"code": ["A", "B", "C"]})
print(df["code"].map({"A": "active", "B": "paused"}).tolist())

topics.title: apply row-wise is a loop in disguise
topics.body: `apply(axis=1)` receives one row at a time and runs Python per row. It is correct for irregular logic, but column arithmetic is faster whenever the operation is elementwise.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [10, 20]})
print(df.apply(lambda row: row["a"] + row["b"], axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: A Series broadcasts down every column
topics.body: A Series lines up with a column axis when you subtract it from a frame, so a per-row vector can be applied to every row without a loop.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
row = pd.Series({"a": 10, "b": 20})
print(df.add(row, axis="columns").values.tolist())

topics.title: where builds a conditional column
topics.body: `where` is a vectorised if: keep the value where the condition holds and substitute otherwise. It is the safe way to add a status column without apply.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"marks": [40, 75]})
df["band"] = df["marks"].where(df["marks"] >= 50, "fail")
print(df["band"].tolist())

debug.broken:

df = pd.DataFrame({"spent": [10, 20], "budget": [0, 40]})

import pandas as pd

import numpy as np

interviewBank.q: When is `apply` the right call?
interviewBank.answer: When the logic is genuinely row-wise and irregular — a lookup across several columns with branching, or a call into library code that takes a row. Even then, `axis=1` is slow; if the operation can be expressed as column arithmetic, that version wins.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `map`, `apply` and `transform` on a Series?
interviewBank.answer: `map` substitutes values (dict, Series or function) elementwise and returns the same shape. `apply` can return an aggregate, so its shape may change. `transform` guarantees the original shape, which is what you need when feeding the result back into the frame.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `assign` and plain column assignment?
interviewBank.answer: `assign` returns a new frame and can be chained inside a pipeline, so the input stays untouched. `df["x"] = ...` mutates the frame in place, which is fine in a script but makes a long chain hard to test.

interviewBank.q: Why does a percentage column produce inf, and how do you prevent it?
interviewBank.answer: Division by zero yields inf (or a warning), and inf then poisons means and charts. Replace zero denominators with NaN before dividing, then decide explicitly whether to fill, drop or flag those rows.

defenseBank.q: Defend this claim: a calculated column should never overwrite its input.
defenseBank.answer: Overwriting destroys the raw value, so a wrong formula cannot be recomputed or audited, and a downstream bug becomes unrecoverable. Keep the input and write the result under a new name; drop the raw column at export if it is genuinely redundant.
steps: State what is lost on overwrite.

defenseBank.q: Your percentage column has inf values and the dashboard shows blank cells. Explain the chain and the fix.
defenseBank.answer: Dividing by zero produces inf, and a later JSON or chart step cannot represent it, so it disappears. Replace the zero denominator with NaN before dividing, then decide explicitly whether to fill, drop or flag those rows.
steps: Name the step that loses it.

learn.title: Column arithmetic creates a column
learn.body: Two Series of the same length combine element by element, and assigning the result adds a column. No loop, no index bookkeeping.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"price": [100, 200], "qty": [2, 3]})
df["total"] = df["price"] * df["qty"]
print(df["total"].tolist())

learn.title: assign keeps the chain readable
learn.body: `assign` returns a new frame with the column added, so a pipeline can stay one expression and the original frame is untouched.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"marks": [40, 80]})
out = df.assign(passed=df["marks"] >= 50)
print(out["passed"].tolist())
print("passed" in df.columns)

learn.title: clip keeps values inside a range
learn.body: `clip(lower, upper)` pins out-of-range values without an if. It is the standard guard before a ratio, a score or a pixel write.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([-5, 50, 150])
print(s.clip(0, 100).tolist())

learn.title: map translates values with a dict
learn.body: `map` looks each value up in a dict, which is how codes become labels. A value missing from the dict becomes NaN.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"code": ["A", "B", "C"]})
print(df["code"].map({"A": "active", "B": "paused"}).tolist())

learn.title: apply row-wise is a loop in disguise
learn.body: `apply(axis=1)` receives one row at a time and runs Python per row. It is correct for irregular logic, but column arithmetic is faster whenever the operation is elementwise.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [10, 20]})
print(df.apply(lambda row: row["a"] + row["b"], axis=1).tolist())

learn.title: A Series broadcasts down every column
learn.body: A Series lines up with a column axis when you subtract it from a frame, so a per-row vector can be applied to every row without a loop.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
row = pd.Series({"a": 10, "b": 20})
print(df.add(row, axis="columns").values.tolist())

modules.title: Sorting, Ranking and Statistics
modules.goal: Order a table, rank inside groups, and read the right descriptive statistic for the question.

topics.title: sort_values orders rows
topics.body: `sort_values` returns a new frame unless `inplace=True`. The index travels with the row, which is why a sorted frame often has an out-of-order index.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Aman", "Riya", "Rahul"], "marks": [85, 92, 78]})
print(df.sort_values("marks", ascending=False)["name"].tolist())

topics.title: Two sort keys, two directions
topics.body: Pass a list of columns and a matching list of booleans. The first key dominates; the second breaks ties.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "marks": [70, 90, 95]})
out = df.sort_values(["city", "marks"], ascending=[True, False])
print(out["marks"].tolist())

topics.title: nlargest skips the full sort
topics.body: `nlargest(n, column)` keeps the top n rows and is cheaper than sorting a million rows to read three.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["A", "B", "C"], "marks": [70, 95, 88]})
print(df.nlargest(2, "marks")["name"].tolist())

topics.title: rank numbers ties explicitly
topics.body: `rank` gives each value a position and lets you choose how ties behave: `method="min"` gives both tied rows rank 1, `dense` gives the next distinct value the next rank.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([90, 90, 70])
print(s.rank(method="min").tolist())
print(s.rank(method="dense").tolist())

topics.title: corr measures linear agreement
topics.body: `corr` returns a matrix from -1 to 1. It measures linear movement only, so a strong curve can still show a correlation near zero.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"hours": [1, 2, 3, 4], "marks": [40, 50, 65, 80]})
print(round(df["hours"].corr(df["marks"]), 3))

topics.title: sort_values decides where NaN goes
topics.body: `na_position` puts missing values first or last. The default is last, which is why a sorted column can hide its gaps at the bottom.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([3.0, None, 1.0])
print(s.sort_values(na_position="first").tolist())

topics.title: rank can be a percentage
topics.body: `rank(pct=True)` returns the position as a share of the rows, which is how a column becomes a percentile score without a second step.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(s.rank(pct=True).round(2).tolist())

topics.title: corrwith compares two frames column by column
topics.body: `corrwith` pairs columns by name and returns one correlation per pair, which is the quickest way to see which features move with a target column.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [3, 2, 1]})
b = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])
print(a.corrwith(b).round(2).to_dict())

topics.title: quantile uses 0 to 1
topics.body: `quantile(0.25)` and `percentile(25)` ask the same question on different scales. Mixing them puts the median at 0.5 or 50 by accident.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(s.quantile(0.5))
print(s.quantile([0.25, 0.75]).tolist())

interviewBank.q: Mean and median differ by a factor of three. What does that tell you?
interviewBank.answer: That the distribution is skewed by large values pulling the mean up — income and response time behave this way. Report the median as typical and the mean as a total-cost figure, and look at the tail before choosing which one the decision needs.

interviewBank.q: What does a correlation of 0.9 not prove?
interviewBank.answer: Causation, and not even linearity beyond the observed range. It can also be produced by a third variable, by a shared trend over time, or by an outlier pair. Plot the scatter before quoting the number.

interviewBank.q: How do you explain a mean that is far above the median?
interviewBank.answer: A long right tail: a few very large values pull the mean up while the median stays at the typical observation. Report both, inspect the top values, and choose the statistic the decision needs.

interviewBank.q: Why is correlation not enough to claim a relationship?
interviewBank.answer: It measures linear co-movement only, can be produced by a third variable or a shared trend, and is sensitive to outliers. Plot the pair and check the relationship inside segments before reporting it.

defenseBank.q: Argue for nlargest over sort_values when the request is "top 5".
defenseBank.answer: The requirement is five rows, not an ordered table. `nlargest` uses a partial selection, so it does not order the other rows at all. Reserve a full sort for when the whole order is the deliverable.
steps: Say what the full sort does that is unused.

defenseBank.q: A dashboard's average is stable but users complain it is wrong. Explain a plausible cause.
defenseBank.answer: The average is likely computed over rows that include duplicates or partial records: a user with three attempts counts three times. Deduplicate to one row per entity before averaging, and state the grain in the metric definition.

modules.title: Missing Data
modules.goal: Find missing values, understand why they are missing, and choose a handling strategy you can defend.

topics.title: isna counts the gaps per column
topics.body: `isna()` returns a boolean frame of the same shape, so summing it gives one count per column and the percentage is one division away.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None], "b": [None, None]})
print(df.isna().sum().tolist())
print(round(df.isna().mean().max() * 100, 1))

topics.title: dropna removes rows by rule
topics.body: With no arguments it drops any row containing a gap; `subset` limits the rule to the columns the analysis actually needs.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "marks": [80, None, 70]})
print(df.dropna().shape[0])
print(df.dropna(subset=["id"]).shape[0])

topics.title: fillna with a decided value
topics.body: Filling with the mean keeps the count and the mean, but shrinks the variance. State which one the analysis needs before choosing the fill value.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10.0, None, 30.0])
print(s.fillna(s.mean()).tolist())
print(s.isna().sum())

topics.title: ffill carries the last known value
topics.body: `ffill` copies the previous non-missing value forward, which is correct for a status that only changes when a new event arrives — not for a measurement.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["active", None, None, "paused"])
print(s.ffill().tolist())

topics.title: interpolate estimates between points
topics.body: Linear interpolation draws a straight line between known values. It suits a smooth series such as temperature, and invents data in a sparse one.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10.0, None, 30.0])
print(s.interpolate().tolist())

topics.title: isna().any(axis=1) finds incomplete rows
topics.body: Reducing the missing mask along the columns answers "which rows have at least one gap", which is the count a data-quality note needs.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None], "b": [None, 2]})
print(df.isna().any(axis=1).tolist())
print(df.isna().all(axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: fillna takes a different rule per column
topics.body: A dict fills each column with its own value, so text and numbers do not share one default that is wrong for both.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"score": [10.0, None], "city": [None, "Pune"]})
print(df.fillna({"score": 0.0, "city": "unknown"}).values.tolist())

topics.title: dropna how decides the rule
topics.body: `how="any"` drops a row with any gap, `how="all"` only when every value is missing. The default is aggressive, so name it.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [None, 1], "b": [None, None]})
print(df.dropna(how="all").shape[0])
print(df.dropna(how="any").shape[0])

topics.title: interpolate can limit the fill distance
topics.body: `limit` and `limit_direction` stop interpolation from bridging a long gap, which keeps an isolated missing point from becoming invented data.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([0.0, None, None, 30.0])
print(s.interpolate(limit=1).tolist())

interviewBank.q: What are the three kinds of missingness, and why does the kind matter?
interviewBank.answer: MCAR (random), MAR (explained by other columns) and MNAR (explained by the missing value itself, such as high earners skipping a salary field). Dropping is safe only under MCAR; otherwise the missingness is signal and should be modelled, for example with a fill plus an `is_missing` flag.

interviewBank.q: Why is filling with the mean often the weakest choice?
interviewBank.answer: It reduces variance, distorts correlations and creates a spike at one value, while pretending the estimate is a real measurement. Median or model-based fills are more robust, and an explicit missing indicator is often more honest than any fill.

interviewBank.q: How do you report handling missing data honestly?
interviewBank.answer: State how many values were missing in each affected column, which rule was applied, and what it changes — an imputed mean reduces variance, and dropping rows changes the population. A reader must be able to see which rows the number came from.

interviewBank.q: Why is `ffill` dangerous on a measurement column?
interviewBank.answer: It asserts the value did not change, which is true for a status and false for a measurement. On a temperature column it creates a plateau and understates the variation, so the statistic describes the fill rule more than the data.

defenseBank.q: A column is 60% missing. Defend your plan.
defenseBank.answer: Above roughly half missing, an imputed column mostly encodes the imputation rule, so I would first check whether the record exists at all (a status or an all-null block). If it does, keep it with an explicit missing flag and exclude it from any average that would be dominated by the fill.
steps: Check whether the gap is structural.
Keep the flag, exclude from averages.

defenseBank.q: Explain why ffill is right for a status column and wrong for a temperature column.
defenseBank.answer: A status is a state that persists until the next event, so the last known value is the true value. A temperature changes continuously, so carrying the last reading forward invents a plateau and understates the variation.

interview.q: What are the three kinds of missingness, and why does the kind matter?
interview.answer: MCAR (random), MAR (explained by other columns) and MNAR (explained by the missing value itself, such as high earners skipping a salary field). Dropping is safe only under MCAR; otherwise the missingness is signal and should be modelled, for example with a fill plus an `is_missing` flag.

interview.q: Why is filling with the mean often the weakest choice?
interview.answer: It reduces variance, distorts correlations and creates a spike at one value, while pretending the estimate is a real measurement. Median or model-based fills are more robust, and an explicit missing indicator is often more honest than any fill.

interview.q: How do you report handling missing data honestly?
interview.answer: State how many values were missing in each affected column, which rule was applied, and what it changes — an imputed mean reduces variance, and dropping rows changes the population. A reader must be able to see which rows the number came from.

interview.q: Why is `ffill` dangerous on a measurement column?
interview.answer: It asserts the value did not change, which is true for a status and false for a measurement. On a temperature column it creates a plateau and understates the variation, so the statistic describes the fill rule more than the data.

defense.q: A column is 60% missing. Defend your plan.
defense.answer: Above roughly half missing, an imputed column mostly encodes the imputation rule, so I would first check whether the record exists at all (a status or an all-null block). defense.q: Explain why ffill is right for a status column and wrong for a temperature column.
defense.answer: A status is a state that persists until the next event, so the last known value is the true value. A temperature changes continuously, so carrying the last reading forward invents a plateau and understates the variation.

interviewBank.q: How do you decide which duplicate to keep?
interviewBank.answer: By the grain and by the newest record: typically order by an updated-at column and keep the last per key. Keeping the first silently keeps the oldest state, which is wrong for slowly changing records.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between an outlier and an invalid value?
interviewBank.answer: An outlier is a real observation far from the rest; an invalid value is impossible — a negative age, a date in the future, a price of zero on a paid order. Validation rules catch the impossible; statistics only flag the unusual.

interviewBank.q: What makes a cleaning step reviewable?
interviewBank.answer: A count before and after, the rule that was applied, and why. "Removed duplicates" is not reviewable; "removed 412 rows where id repeated, keeping the newest by updated_at" is.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer IQR over a fixed threshold for outliers?
interviewBank.answer: The IQR adapts to the column's own spread and ignores the tail when computing the bounds, so one extreme value cannot widen the threshold enough to hide itself. A fixed threshold requires knowing the domain.

defenseBank.q: Defend writing a validation report before removing any row.
defenseBank.answer: Removal is irreversible and hides the cause. A report that counts duplicates, invalid values and outliers per column shows whether the pipeline is broken upstream, and gives a number to compare after the fix instead of a silently smaller table.

defenseBank.q: A teammate drops every row outside 3 standard deviations. What is the problem?
defenseBank.answer: The rule assumes a roughly normal distribution and is itself distorted by the extreme values it targets; on a skewed column it can delete a large legitimate tail. Use IQR or a domain threshold, and say which rows were removed.

modules.title: Strings and Regular Expressions
modules.goal: Clean and extract text with the .str accessor and regex, without a Python loop.

topics.title: str.contains filters text
topics.body: `contains` returns a boolean mask; `case=False` and `regex=True` are the two arguments that decide whether a search is literal or a pattern.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"email": ["a@gmail.com", "b@yahoo.com"]})
print(df["email"].str.contains("gmail", case=False).tolist())

topics.title: str.extract pulls a group out
topics.body: A capture group in the pattern becomes a column. `expand=False` returns a Series when there is exactly one group.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"email": ["a@gmail.com", "b@yahoo.com"]})
df["domain"] = df["email"].str.extract(r"@(\w+)\.")
print(df["domain"].tolist())

topics.title: str.split expands into columns
topics.body: `split(pat, expand=True)` turns one text column into several, which is how a "city, state" field becomes two usable columns.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"where": ["Pune, MH", "Delhi, DL"]})
parts = df["where"].str.split(", ", expand=True)
print(parts.shape)
print(parts[0].tolist())

topics.title: str.len measures the text
topics.body: Length is a cheap validation: a phone number column with lengths other than 10 is wrong before any regex.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"phone": ["9876543210", "98765"]})
print(df["phone"].str.len().tolist())

topics.title: Regex cleans a phone number
topics.body: `replace` with `regex=True` removes every non-digit in one pass, then the length check tells you which numbers are still invalid.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"phone": ["+91 98765-43210", "(022) 1234 5678"]})
digits = df["phone"].str.replace(r"\D", "", regex=True)
print(digits.str.len().tolist())

topics.title: zfill pads numeric-looking ids
topics.body: `str.zfill` pads to a fixed width, which makes ids sort and join consistently instead of mixing 7 and 0007.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([7, 42]).astype(str)
print(s.str.zfill(4).tolist())

topics.title: str.cat joins two text columns
topics.body: `str.cat` concatenates columns with a separator and handles missing values, replacing the string `+` that fails on NaN.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"first": ["Aman"], "last": ["Sharma"]})
print(df["first"].str.cat(df["last"], sep=" ").tolist())

topics.title: str.slice takes positions
topics.body: `str.slice(0, 2)` takes characters by position, which is the quickest read of a fixed-width code such as a state prefix.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["MH-PUN-01", "DL-DEL-02"])
print(s.str.slice(0, 2).tolist())

topics.title: str.get reads one piece of a split
topics.body: `str.split(...).str.get(1)` extracts one element without expanding the column, so the frame shape stays the same.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["pune|MH", "delhi|DL"])
print(s.str.split("|").str.get(1).tolist())

interviewBank.q: Why prefer a vectorised .str call over a list comprehension of string methods?
interviewBank.answer: The `.str` accessor handles missing values as NaN instead of raising, runs the same compiled loop over the column, and keeps the index. A comprehension needs its own None handling and rebuilds a Series.

interviewBank.q: When is a regex the wrong tool?
interviewBank.answer: When the format is structured — parse JSON, split on a fixed delimiter, or use a real date parser. Regex for HTML or nested syntax becomes unreadable and wrong at the edges; use the parser that owns the format.

interviewBank.q: When do you stop using `.str` and parse instead?
interviewBank.answer: When the text is a serialised structure — JSON, HTML, a nested field. Regex over it is unreadable and breaks on the first nesting; use the parser that owns the format, then hand the fields to Pandas.

interviewBank.q: Why normalise case and whitespace before a join on text?
interviewBank.answer: Joins compare exactly, so "Pune" and "pune " never match and the join silently drops rows. Normalising both sides first makes the match reflect the data rather than the formatting.

defenseBank.q: Defend normalising text before grouping.
defenseBank.answer: Group keys compare exactly, so "Pune", "pune" and "Pune " become three groups and every aggregate is split three ways. Normalising case and whitespace first makes the group count match the real number of cities.

defenseBank.q: A phone column has 8, 10 and 12 digit values. What do you report?
defenseBank.answer: That the column has three length populations, which usually means a country code or a missing prefix, not bad data. Report the counts per length before changing anything, then normalise with an explicit rule.

interview.answer: When the text is a serialised structure — JSON, HTML, a nested field. Regex over it is unreadable and breaks on the first nesting; use the parser that owns the format, then hand the fields to Pandas.

interview.q: Why normalise case and whitespace before a join on text?
interview.answer: Joins compare exactly, so "Pune" and "pune " never match and the join silently drops rows. Normalising both sides first makes the match reflect the data rather than the formatting.

defense.q: Defend normalising text before grouping.
defense.answer: Group keys compare exactly, so "Pune", "pune" and "Pune " become three groups and every aggregate is split three ways. Normalising case and whitespace first makes the group count match the real number of cities.

defense.q: A phone column has 8, 10 and 12 digit values. What do you report?

modules.title: Importing and Exporting Data
modules.goal: Read and write CSV, JSON and SQL without losing types, and stream a file that does not fit in memory.

topics.title: read_csv with an explicit separator
topics.body: `read_csv` splits on a comma by default. A semicolon or tab file that is not declared arrives as one wide text column.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "name;marks\nAman;85\nRiya;92"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), sep=";")
print(df.shape)
print(df["marks"].sum())

topics.title: Read only the columns you need
topics.body: `usecols` and `dtype` cut memory at the source: a wide export becomes a small typed frame without a post-load clean-up.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "id,name,marks\n1,Aman,85\n2,Riya,92"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), usecols=["name", "marks"], dtype={"marks": "int16"})
print(df.columns.tolist())
print(df["marks"].dtype)

topics.title: to_csv without the index
topics.body: By default the index is written as an unnamed first column. `index=False` is what stops a round trip from growing a column each time.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]})
print(df.to_csv(index=False).strip().split("\n"))

topics.title: JSON arrives as records
topics.body: A JSON array of objects becomes rows directly; nested objects need `json_normalize` to become columns.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

records = [{"id": 1, "meta": {"city": "Pune"}}, {"id": 2, "meta": {"city": "Delhi"}}]
df = pd.json_normalize(records)
print(df.columns.tolist())

topics.title: read_sql runs inside the database
topics.body: `read_sql` sends the query and builds the frame from the result, so filtering happens in SQL instead of after a full load.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("create table marks (name text, mark integer)")
con.executemany("insert into marks values (?, ?)", [("Aman", 85), ("Riya", 92)])
print(pd.read_sql("select name from marks where mark > 90", con)["name"].tolist())

topics.title: na_values declares the sentinels
topics.body: A CSV often encodes missing data as "NA", "-" or "999". `na_values` names them at load time, so they arrive as NaN instead of as a category or a number.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "v\n10\nNA"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), na_values=["NA"])
print(df["v"].isna().tolist())

topics.title: nrows reads a sample of a big file
topics.body: `nrows` reads the first n data rows, which is enough to check the columns and dtypes of a file that would take minutes to parse fully.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "a,b\n1,2\n3,4\n5,6"
print(pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), nrows=1).shape)

topics.title: to_json orient chooses the shape
topics.body: `orient="records"` writes one object per row, which is what an API expects. The default is column-oriented and reads very differently.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [2]})
print(df.to_json(orient="records"))

topics.title: index_col moves a column into the index at load
topics.body: `index_col` avoids a later `set_index`, and it keeps the column out of the data from the start, which is why an id often belongs there.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

print(pd.read_csv(StringIO("id,v\n1,10\n"), index_col="id").index.tolist())

import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "id,name,marks\n1,Aman,85\n2,Riya,92\n"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), usecols=["name", "marks"], dtype={"marks": int})
print(df["marks"].mean())

interviewBank.q: How do you read a 20 GB CSV on a laptop?
interviewBank.answer: In chunks: `read_csv(..., chunksize=1_000_000)` and aggregate each chunk into a small result, so peak memory is one chunk. If the file is columnar, convert once to Parquet and read only the needed columns.

interviewBank.q: What does `parse_dates` change about later work?
interviewBank.answer: It makes the column datetime64, which enables `.dt`, resampling, rolling windows and date arithmetic. Without it the column is text, comparisons are lexicographic and `resample` raises.

interviewBank.q: How do you make a CSV load reproducible?
interviewBank.answer: Pin the contract: `sep`, `dtype`, `parse_dates`, `na_values`, `usecols`. Then the same file produces the same frame on every machine, and a change in the source fails at the boundary instead of in a later mean.

interviewBank.q: Why is a Parquet export often preferred to CSV for downstream analysis?
interviewBank.answer: Parquet stores the schema and the types, reads only the columns requested, and is far faster to parse at size. CSV is portable and human-readable, which is the reason it is still the interchange default.

defenseBank.q: Argue for pinning a dtype map in a production loader.
defenseBank.answer: An inferred dtype can change when the data changes — one new blank cell turns an integer column into float and the join key stops matching. An explicit map makes the contract fail at load instead of at analysis.

defenseBank.q: When is exporting to CSV the wrong deliverable?
defenseBank.answer: When the consumer is another program that needs types and speed, or when the data is large: CSV loses dtypes, is slow to parse and cannot hold nested or binary values. Parquet keeps the schema and reads only the columns asked for.

learn.title: read_csv with an explicit separator
learn.body: `read_csv` splits on a comma by default. A semicolon or tab file that is not declared arrives as one wide text column.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "name;marks\nAman;85\nRiya;92"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), sep=";")
print(df.shape)
print(df["marks"].sum())

learn.title: Read only the columns you need
learn.body: `usecols` and `dtype` cut memory at the source: a wide export becomes a small typed frame without a post-load clean-up.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "id,name,marks\n1,Aman,85\n2,Riya,92"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), usecols=["name", "marks"], dtype={"marks": "int16"})
print(df.columns.tolist())
print(df["marks"].dtype)

learn.title: to_csv without the index
learn.body: By default the index is written as an unnamed first column. `index=False` is what stops a round trip from growing a column each time.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]})
print(df.to_csv(index=False).strip().split("\n"))

learn.title: JSON arrives as records
learn.body: A JSON array of objects becomes rows directly; nested objects need `json_normalize` to become columns.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

records = [{"id": 1, "meta": {"city": "Pune"}}, {"id": 2, "meta": {"city": "Delhi"}}]
df = pd.json_normalize(records)
print(df.columns.tolist())

learn.title: read_sql runs inside the database
learn.body: `read_sql` sends the query and builds the frame from the result, so filtering happens in SQL instead of after a full load.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("create table marks (name text, mark integer)")
con.executemany("insert into marks values (?, ?)", [("Aman", 85), ("Riya", 92)])
print(pd.read_sql("select name from marks where mark > 90", con)["name"].tolist())

learn.title: na_values declares the sentinels
learn.body: A CSV often encodes missing data as "NA", "-" or "999". `na_values` names them at load time, so they arrive as NaN instead of as a category or a number.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "v\n10\nNA"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), na_values=["NA"])
print(df["v"].isna().tolist())

learn.title: nrows reads a sample of a big file
learn.body: `nrows` reads the first n data rows, which is enough to check the columns and dtypes of a file that would take minutes to parse fully.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "a,b\n1,2\n3,4\n5,6"
print(pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), nrows=1).shape)

learn.title: to_json orient chooses the shape
learn.body: `orient="records"` writes one object per row, which is what an API expects. The default is column-oriented and reads very differently.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [2]})
print(df.to_json(orient="records"))

learn.title: index_col moves a column into the index at load
learn.body: `index_col` avoids a later `set_index`, and it keeps the column out of the data from the start, which is why an id often belongs there.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

print(pd.read_csv(StringIO("id,v\n1,10\n"), index_col="id").index.tolist())

modules.title: Merging, Joining and Concatenation
modules.goal: Combine tables by key or by stacking, and prove the row count did what you intended.

topics.title: merge joins on a shared key
topics.body: `merge` matches rows by key and keeps the columns of both sides. The default `how="inner"` keeps only keys present in both.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

users = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "name": ["Aman", "Riya"]})
marks = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 3], "mark": [85, 92]})
print(users.merge(marks, on="id").shape[0])

topics.title: A left join keeps every row on the left
topics.body: `how="left"` never drops a left row; unmatched keys get NaN on the right. That is the shape of a "who has not done it" question.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

users = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "name": ["Aman", "Riya"]})
marks = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "mark": [85]})
out = users.merge(marks, on="id", how="left")
print(out["mark"].isna().tolist())

topics.title: indicator names where each row came from
topics.body: `indicator=True` adds `_merge` with `both`, `left_only` or `right_only`, which turns an audit question into a filter.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"id": [2, 3]})
out = a.merge(b, on="id", how="outer", indicator=True)
print(out["_merge"].value_counts().to_dict())

topics.title: concat stacks rows
topics.body: `concat` glues tables along an axis without matching keys. `ignore_index=True` renumbers the result so the old labels do not repeat.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

jan = pd.DataFrame({"sales": [10]})
feb = pd.DataFrame({"sales": [20]})
out = pd.concat([jan, feb], ignore_index=True)
print(out["sales"].tolist())
print(out.index.tolist())

topics.title: validate refuses a fan-out
topics.body: A duplicate key on either side multiplies rows. `validate="one_to_one"` raises instead of shipping a table that is quietly bigger.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "x": [10, 20]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "y": [1, 2]})
print(a.merge(b, on="id", validate="one_to_one").shape[0])

topics.title: suffixes name the collision
topics.body: When both sides have a column of the same name, `suffixes` decides the two new names. Naming them explicitly keeps a report readable.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "v": [10]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "v": [20]})
out = a.merge(b, on="id", suffixes=("_left", "_right"))
print(out.columns.tolist())

topics.title: concat stacks columns with axis=1
topics.body: `axis=1` places frames side by side and aligns them by index. Misaligned labels produce NaN rows, which is the sign the indexes did not agree.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"y": [2]})
print(pd.concat([a, b], axis=1).shape)

topics.title: merge on the index needs no key column
topics.body: With `left_index` and `right_index` the join uses labels, which is how two tables already indexed by the same key are combined without a reset.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1]}, index=["k"])
b = pd.DataFrame({"y": [2]}, index=["k"])
print(a.merge(b, left_index=True, right_index=True).values.tolist())

topics.title: indicator turns a mystery into a filter
topics.body: `_merge` labels each row as `both`, `left_only` or `right_only`. Filtering `left_only` is the "who never matched" report.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"id": [2]})
out = a.merge(b, on="id", how="left", indicator=True)
print(out["_merge"].tolist())

interviewBank.q: Why does a merge sometimes return more rows than the left table?
interviewBank.answer: Because the key is not unique on the right: each match produces a row, so one left row with three right matches becomes three. That is a fan-out, and `validate` is the check that catches it before the numbers are trusted.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between merge and join?
interviewBank.answer: `merge` is the general, key-based operation with `on`, `how` and `validate`. `join` is a convenience that joins on the index by default. For anything beyond a simple index join, `merge` is the explicit choice.

interviewBank.q: How do you prove a join did not change the grain?
interviewBank.answer: Record the row count and the key's uniqueness on both sides, then compare the result with the expected relationship: one-to-one keeps the count, one-to-many multiplies it by the matches. `validate` turns the expectation into an assertion.

interviewBank.q: What is the risk of `how="outer"` on a large table?
interviewBank.answer: It keeps unmatched keys from both sides, so the result grows and the NaN columns mix two different kinds of missingness — a genuinely absent record and a record that exists but has no value. Report the counts of each separately.

defenseBank.q: Explain why you check the row count before and after every join.
defenseBank.answer: A join can multiply or drop rows without any error. Comparing counts before and after is the cheapest proof that the relationship was what I assumed, and when it changes I know the key is not unique.

defenseBank.q: When is concat the right tool instead of merge?
defenseBank.answer: When the tables are the same shape and represent the same entity over time or source — monthly files, two regions. Merge combines different attributes of one entity; concat extends the rows of one table.

projectLab.title: Join audit
projectLab.body: Build a reusable join that reports the row count before and after, the unmatched keys, and refuses a fan-out.
steps: Print unmatched counts and the delta.

defense.q: Explain why you check the row count before and after every join.
defense.answer: A join can multiply or drop rows without any error. Comparing counts before and after is the cheapest proof that the relationship was what I assumed, and when it changes I know the key is not unique.

defense.q: When is concat the right tool instead of merge?
defense.answer: When the tables are the same shape and represent the same entity over time or source — monthly files, two regions. Merge combines different attributes of one entity; concat extends the rows of one table.

modules.title: GroupBy and Aggregation
modules.goal: Split a table by a key, compute per-group answers, and put them back beside the original rows.

topics.title: groupby splits, then aggregates
topics.body: `groupby(key)` groups rows with the same key; a reduction then returns one value per group instead of per row.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
print(df.groupby("city")["sales"].sum().to_dict())

topics.title: agg asks several questions at once
topics.body: Passing a list of function names returns one column per function. Named aggregation gives those columns the names the report needs.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
g = df.groupby("city").agg(total=("sales", "sum"), n=("sales", "size"))
print(g.loc["Pune"].tolist())

topics.title: transform keeps the row count
topics.body: `transform` returns a value per original row, so a group mean can be attached back and used in a per-row comparison.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
df["avg"] = df.groupby("city")["sales"].transform("mean")
print(df["avg"].tolist())

topics.title: filter keeps whole groups
topics.body: `filter` takes a function of the group and returns the rows of the groups that pass, which is different from filtering rows.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
out = df.groupby("city").filter(lambda g: g["sales"].sum() > 20)
print(out["city"].unique().tolist())

topics.title: Two keys make a MultiIndex result
topics.body: Grouping by two columns returns a Series indexed by both keys. `unstack` turns the second key into columns for a report.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "year": [2025, 2026, 2026], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
out = df.groupby(["city", "year"])["sales"].sum().unstack(fill_value=0)
print(out.columns.tolist())

topics.title: as_index=False keeps the key as a column
topics.body: By default the group key becomes the index. `as_index=False` keeps it as a column, which is what a flat export or a chart expects.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune"], "v": [1, 2]})
out = df.groupby("city", as_index=False)["v"].sum()
print(out.columns.tolist())

topics.title: dropna=False keeps the missing key
topics.body: Rows with a missing group key are dropped by default, so the totals shrink. Keeping them shows that the key itself is incomplete.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", None], "v": [1, 2]})
print(len(df.groupby("city")["v"].sum()))
print(len(df.groupby("city", dropna=False)["v"].sum()))

topics.title: ngroup numbers the groups
topics.body: `ngroup()` returns a group number per row, which is how a categorical segment becomes a compact integer feature for a model.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["b", "a", "b"]})
print(df.groupby("city").ngroup().tolist())

topics.title: size counts rows, count counts values
topics.body: `size` includes missing values, `count` does not. On a sparse column the two answers differ, and the wrong one overstates the evidence.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "a"], "v": [1.0, None]})
out = df.groupby("g").agg(n=("v", "size"), filled=("v", "count"))
print(out.values.tolist())

interviewBank.q: What does groupby actually do internally?
interviewBank.answer: Split the rows into groups by the key, apply the function to each group, combine the results into one object indexed by the key. The split is why a groupby on a high-cardinality key is expensive, and why the result is indexed by that key.

interviewBank.q: When do you use transform instead of agg?
interviewBank.answer: When the answer must line up with the original rows: adding a group mean to each row, or comparing a row against its group. `agg` collapses each group to one row; `transform` returns one value per input row.

interviewBank.q: Why report a group size beside a group mean?
interviewBank.answer: A mean over one or two rows has no meaningful spread and cannot be compared with a mean over thousands. The size column lets the reader see which conclusions are supported and which are anecdote.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `agg` and `transform` in one example?
interviewBank.answer: `agg("mean")` collapses each city to a single row — a report. `transform("mean")` returns the city mean on every original row, so it can be compared with the row's own value to find above-average records.

defenseBank.q: A groupby mean looks wrong because one group has a single row. What do you do?
defenseBank.answer: Report the group size beside the mean, because a mean of one observation has no spread and is not comparable. Filter or flag groups below a minimum count, and say the threshold in the output.

defenseBank.q: Explain the difference between dropping missing keys and keeping them in a groupby.
defenseBank.answer: By default `groupby` drops rows whose key is missing, so the totals silently shrink. `dropna=False` keeps them as a group, which is right when the missing key itself is a finding.
steps: Give the flag and when to use it.
