learn.title: groupby splits, then aggregates
learn.body: `groupby(key)` groups rows with the same key; a reduction then returns one value per group instead of per row.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
print(df.groupby("city")["sales"].sum().to_dict())

learn.title: agg asks several questions at once
learn.body: Passing a list of function names returns one column per function. Named aggregation gives those columns the names the report needs.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
g = df.groupby("city").agg(total=("sales", "sum"), n=("sales", "size"))
print(g.loc["Pune"].tolist())

learn.title: transform keeps the row count
learn.body: `transform` returns a value per original row, so a group mean can be attached back and used in a per-row comparison.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
df["avg"] = df.groupby("city")["sales"].transform("mean")
print(df["avg"].tolist())

learn.title: filter keeps whole groups
learn.body: `filter` takes a function of the group and returns the rows of the groups that pass, which is different from filtering rows.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
out = df.groupby("city").filter(lambda g: g["sales"].sum() > 20)
print(out["city"].unique().tolist())

learn.title: Two keys make a MultiIndex result
learn.body: Grouping by two columns returns a Series indexed by both keys. `unstack` turns the second key into columns for a report.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "year": [2025, 2026, 2026], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
out = df.groupby(["city", "year"])["sales"].sum().unstack(fill_value=0)
print(out.columns.tolist())

learn.title: as_index=False keeps the key as a column
learn.body: By default the group key becomes the index. `as_index=False` keeps it as a column, which is what a flat export or a chart expects.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune"], "v": [1, 2]})
out = df.groupby("city", as_index=False)["v"].sum()
print(out.columns.tolist())

learn.title: dropna=False keeps the missing key
learn.body: Rows with a missing group key are dropped by default, so the totals shrink. Keeping them shows that the key itself is incomplete.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", None], "v": [1, 2]})
print(len(df.groupby("city")["v"].sum()))
print(len(df.groupby("city", dropna=False)["v"].sum()))

learn.title: ngroup numbers the groups
learn.body: `ngroup()` returns a group number per row, which is how a categorical segment becomes a compact integer feature for a model.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["b", "a", "b"]})
print(df.groupby("city").ngroup().tolist())

learn.title: size counts rows, count counts values
learn.body: `size` includes missing values, `count` does not. On a sparse column the two answers differ, and the wrong one overstates the evidence.
learn.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "a"], "v": [1.0, None]})
out = df.groupby("g").agg(n=("v", "size"), filled=("v", "count"))
print(out.values.tolist())

modules.goal: Move between long and wide layouts, and choose the reshape that answers the question.

topics.title: pivot_table builds a cross-tab
topics.body: `pivot_table` aggregates by default, so duplicate key combinations do not raise. Rows, columns and values are named explicitly.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "year": [2025, 2026, 2026], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
t = df.pivot_table(index="city", columns="year", values="sales", aggfunc="sum")
print(t.shape)
print(t.loc["Pune"].tolist())

topics.title: melt turns columns into rows
topics.body: `melt` is the inverse of a pivot: wide columns become a key column plus a value column, which is the shape plotting and groupby prefer.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune"], "2025": [10], "2026": [20]})
long = df.melt(id_vars="city", var_name="year", value_name="sales")
print(long.shape)
print(long["year"].tolist())

topics.title: crosstab counts combinations
topics.body: `crosstab` counts how often each pair of values occurs. `normalize="index"` turns counts into a row-wise share.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "passed": [True, False, True]})
t = pd.crosstab(df["city"], df["passed"], normalize="index").round(2)
print(t.loc["Pune"].tolist())

topics.title: explode expands a list column
topics.body: A cell holding a list becomes one row per element with `explode`, which is how tags and multi-value fields become analysable.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "tags": [["py", "sql"], ["py"]]})
out = df.explode("tags")
print(out.shape[0])
print(out["tags"].tolist())

topics.title: get_dummies encodes categories
topics.body: One-hot columns turn a category into numbers a model can read. `dtype=int` keeps the output from doubling memory as booleans.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi"]})
out = pd.get_dummies(df["city"], dtype=int)
print(out.columns.tolist())
print(out.values.tolist())

topics.title: margins adds the totals row
topics.body: `margins=True` appends an All row and column, so a pivot table carries its own totals instead of a second computation.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "year": [2025, 2026, 2026], "v": [1, 2, 3]})
t = df.pivot_table(index="city", columns="year", values="v", aggfunc="sum", margins=True, fill_value=0)
print(t.index.tolist())

topics.title: stack and unstack are inverses
topics.body: `stack` moves the innermost column level into the index; `unstack` moves it back. A round trip is a good way to prove a reshape lost nothing.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [2]}, index=["r"])
long = df.stack()
print(long.tolist())
print(long.unstack().values.tolist())

topics.title: wide_to_long needs a stub name
topics.body: `wide_to_long` collects columns that share a prefix, so `sale_2025`, `sale_2026` become one value column with the year kept in a new column.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "sale_2025": [10], "sale_2026": [20]})
long = pd.wide_to_long(df, stubnames="sale", i="id", j="year", sep="_")
print(long["sale"].tolist())

topics.title: crosstab can show shares
topics.body: `normalize="columns"` divides each column by its total, so a crosstab reports a share rather than a count — the difference between 200 rows and 20%.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": ["x", "x", "y"], "b": [1, 1, 0]})
print(pd.crosstab(df["a"], df["b"], normalize="columns").round(2).values.tolist())

interviewBank.q: When do you want long data instead of wide?
interviewBank.answer: When the analysis groups or plots by a variable that is currently spread across columns — year, metric, region. Long data has one value column and one key column, which is what groupby, seaborn and most model APIs expect.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between pivot and pivot_table?
interviewBank.answer: `pivot` only reshapes unique index/column pairs and raises on duplicates. `pivot_table` aggregates duplicates with `aggfunc`, so it is the safe choice on real data.

interviewBank.q: What makes a dataset tidy?
interviewBank.answer: One row per observation, one column per variable, one value per cell. Wide monthly columns violate it because the month is a variable spread across headers; melting restores the rule and makes grouping and plotting direct.

interviewBank.q: Why does a pivot show NaN where you expect zero?
interviewBank.answer: The combination does not exist in the data, so there is no group to aggregate. `fill_value=0` states the business meaning — no activity — instead of leaving the reader to guess between absent and unknown.

defenseBank.q: Defend storing a clean dataset in long format.
defenseBank.answer: Long format is additive: a new month is new rows, not a new column, so no code or schema changes. It also makes the metric a value instead of a column name, which is what groupby and plotting need.

defenseBank.q: A pivot table has a NaN where you expect a zero. Explain and fix.
defenseBank.answer: The combination simply does not exist in the data, so there is no row to aggregate and pandas leaves NaN. `fill_value=0` states the business meaning — no activity — instead of implying unknown.

defense.q: Defend storing a clean dataset in long format.
defense.answer: Long format is additive: a new month is new rows, not a new column, so no code or schema changes. It also makes the metric a value instead of a column name, which is what groupby and plotting need.

defense.q: A pivot table has a NaN where you expect a zero. Explain and fix.
defense.answer: The combination simply does not exist in the data, so there is no row to aggregate and pandas leaves NaN. `fill_value=0` states the business meaning — no activity — instead of implying unknown.
steps: Say why the cell is NaN.

modules.title: Datetime and Time Series
modules.goal: Parse dates, extract parts, resample a series and compute rolling windows.

topics.title: Parse once, then use dt
topics.body: `to_datetime` makes the column datetime64, and the `.dt` accessor then exposes year, month, weekday and formatting without another parse.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"at": ["2026-01-05", "2026-02-10"]})
df["at"] = pd.to_datetime(df["at"])
print(df["at"].dt.month.tolist())
print(df["at"].dt.day_name().tolist())

topics.title: date_range generates the calendar
topics.body: `date_range` builds an index of dates with a frequency. `freq="W"` marks weekly boundaries and `"B"` business days, which is how a gap-free series is built.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

idx = pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=3, freq="D")
print(idx.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist())

topics.title: resample aggregates by period
topics.body: With a DatetimeIndex, `resample("M")` groups rows into months and applies a reduction — the time-series version of groupby.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

idx = pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-05", "2026-01-20", "2026-02-02"])
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 5], index=idx)
print(s.resample("MS").sum().tolist())

topics.title: rolling smooths a series
topics.body: `rolling(2).mean()` averages each point with the previous one. The first window is incomplete, so it starts as NaN.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10.0, 20.0, 30.0])
print(s.rolling(2).mean().round(1).tolist())

topics.title: shift compares with the previous period
topics.body: `shift(1)` moves values down one row, so subtracting it gives the change from the previous period without a loop.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([100, 110, 99])
print(s.diff().tolist())

topics.title: strftime formats a datetime column
topics.body: `.dt.strftime` turns timestamps into the exact text a report needs, and it is the safest way to compare a month label across two sources.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(["2026-01-05"]))
print(s.dt.strftime("%b %Y").tolist())

topics.title: DateOffset moves by calendar units
topics.body: `pd.DateOffset(months=1)` respects month lengths, unlike adding 30 days. It is the correct arithmetic for billing cycles and renewals.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

interviewBank.q: Why is resampling different from groupby on a month column?
interviewBank.answer: Resample knows the calendar: it produces every period in the range, including empty ones, and respects frequency rules such as business days and month starts. Grouping on an extracted month only returns the months that exist.

interviewBank.q: What does `rolling(7)` do at the start of a series?
interviewBank.answer: The first six windows are incomplete, so the default result is NaN. `min_periods=1` computes with whatever is available, which changes the shape of the early values and should be a stated decision.

interviewBank.q: Why does resample produce months that a groupby would miss?
interviewBank.answer: Resample generates the calendar for the range, including empty periods, so a gap is visible as a row. Grouping on an extracted month only returns the months that have data, which hides the gap.

interviewBank.q: What does a rolling window assume about the data?
interviewBank.answer: That the index is evenly spaced and ordered, and that the window's rows are comparable periods. On uneven sampling or duplicate timestamps the window mixes different amounts of time, so the mean is not comparable across rows.

defenseBank.q: Defend converting to datetime at load rather than when a chart needs it.
defenseBank.answer: The parse either succeeds once or fails once, at the boundary, with one dtype for the column. Parsing later means every consumer has to remember, and mixed formats can parse differently in two places.

defenseBank.q: A monthly revenue chart shows a dip every February. How do you explain it?
defenseBank.answer: February is shorter, so a monthly sum compares unequal periods. Compare a daily average, or use a same-length window or year-over-year comparison before calling it a decline.

modules.title: Advanced Pandas
modules.goal: Use MultiIndex, categoricals, pipelines and index alignment deliberately instead of avoiding them.

topics.title: A MultiIndex is a key of several levels
topics.body: Grouping by two keys produces a MultiIndex. `get_level_values` reads one level back as a flat index.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "year": [2025, 2026, 2026], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
s = df.groupby(["city", "year"])["sales"].sum()
print(s.index.nlevels)
print(s.index.get_level_values("year").tolist())

topics.title: xs selects one level
topics.body: `xs` cross-sections a MultiIndex at one level, returning the remaining levels without a full reset.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "year": [2025, 2026, 2026], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
s = df.groupby(["city", "year"])["sales"].sum()
print(s.xs(2026, level="year").tolist())

topics.title: Categorical makes the order explicit
topics.body: A categorical dtype knows its categories and whether order matters, so sorting and plotting follow the domain order instead of alphabetical.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["medium", "low", "high"], dtype=pd.CategoricalDtype(["low", "medium", "high"], ordered=True))
print(s.sort_values().tolist())

topics.title: pipe keeps a pipeline readable
topics.body: `pipe` passes the frame into a function, so a sequence of named steps reads top to bottom instead of nesting calls.

topics.title: combine_first fills holes from another table
topics.body: `combine_first` takes the first non-missing value across two aligned tables, which is how a corrected override is merged over a base record.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.Series([1.0, None, 3.0])
b = pd.Series([9.0, 2.0, 9.0])
print(a.combine_first(b).tolist())

topics.title: swaplevel exchanges two levels
topics.body: A MultiIndex keeps the level names, and `swaplevel` exchanges their order so the report sorts by the other dimension without rebuilding the groupby.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune"], "year": [2026], "v": [1]})
s = df.groupby(["city", "year"])["v"].sum()
print(s.swaplevel().index.names)

topics.title: pd.NA is the missing scalar
topics.body: `pd.NA` is the missing value of the nullable dtypes, distinct from `np.nan`. `isna()` recognises both, which is why a test should use it rather than an equality check.
topics.code:

s = pd.Series([1, pd.NA], dtype="Int64")
print(s.isna().tolist())
print(s.fillna(0).tolist())

topics.title: pipe can pass arguments
topics.body: `pipe` forwards extra arguments to the function, so one reusable step can be parameterised without a lambda.

topics.title: query can read a local variable
topics.body: An `@name` inside a query refers to a Python variable, which lets a threshold come from config while the condition stays a readable string.

interviewBank.q: What problem does a MultiIndex solve, and what does it cost?
interviewBank.answer: It keeps several key levels without repeating values or inventing a concatenated string key, and it supports cross-sections with `xs`. The cost is verbosity: most operations need `reset_index` or `level=` to be explicit, and a partially selected frame can surprise a reader.

interviewBank.q: Why is `pipe` better than one long chained expression?
interviewBank.answer: Each step becomes a named function that can be tested alone, and the reader sees the order of transformations. A chain of `.assign` and `.query` is fine until a step needs branching or a docstring.

interviewBank.q: When is a MultiIndex worth the verbosity?
interviewBank.answer: When a result is genuinely two-dimensional and the second dimension is a category such as year, and when cross-sections with `xs` replace repeated filtering. For a single flat report, `reset_index` is easier to read.

interviewBank.q: What does Copy-on-Write change for a learner?
interviewBank.answer: A slice behaves like a copy for writes: modifying a derived frame no longer changes the parent silently, and chained assignment either fails or does nothing. The fix is one `.loc` call on the frame you intend to change.

defenseBank.q: Defend using categoricals for a status column.
defenseBank.answer: Status has a small fixed vocabulary, so codes save memory and the ordered categories make sorting and plotting correct. The constraint also fails loudly when a new value arrives instead of silently widening the column.

defenseBank.q: A pipeline has eight chained methods. When do you split it?
defenseBank.answer: When a step needs a comment longer than its name, when it is reused by another report, or when it is the only step that needs a test. Those are the points where a named function with `pipe` pays for itself.

modules.title: Exploratory Data Analysis
modules.goal: Profile a dataset, find the patterns worth reporting, and turn each one into a sentence a stakeholder can act on.

topics.title: Start with the distribution, not the mean
topics.body: Mean, median, std and quartiles together describe shape. A mean far above the median is the first sign of a long right tail.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"spend": [100, 120, 130, 900]})
print(round(df["spend"].mean(), 1), df["spend"].median())
print(round(df["spend"].quantile(0.75), 1))

topics.title: Value counts reveal the busy categories
topics.body: Counting a category before grouping tells you which groups are large enough to compare and which are noise.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"course": ["Python", "Python", "SQL", "Python"]})
counts = df["course"].value_counts()
print(counts.to_dict())
print(round(counts.max() / counts.sum() * 100, 1))

topics.title: Correlation is a starting question
topics.body: A correlation matrix ranks candidate relationships. Read it as "what to plot next", never as a finding on its own.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"hours": [1, 2, 3, 4], "marks": [40, 50, 65, 80], "sleep": [8, 7, 7, 6]})
c = df.corr().round(2)
print(c.loc["marks"].to_dict())

topics.title: Group by the dimension in the question
topics.body: An EDA finding is usually a comparison: this segment versus that one. Group by the segment and report count plus rate, never a bare average.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "passed": [True, False, True]})
out = df.groupby("city")["passed"].agg(["count", "mean"])
print(out.loc["Pune"].round(2).tolist())

topics.title: cut turns a number into a band
topics.body: `cut` bins a continuous column into labelled intervals, which is how an age or spend distribution becomes a readable table.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

ages = pd.Series([12, 25, 41, 63])
bands = pd.cut(ages, bins=[0, 18, 35, 60, 100], labels=["teen", "young", "adult", "senior"])
print(bands.value_counts().to_dict())

topics.title: skew tells you which way the tail runs
topics.body: `skew()` is positive when the long tail is on the right and negative when it is on the left. It quantifies what a mean far above the median already hinted at.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

print(round(float(pd.Series([1, 1, 1, 100]).skew()), 2))
print(round(float(pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4]).skew()), 2))

topics.title: corr takes a method
topics.body: Pearson measures linear agreement; Spearman ranks the values first, so it survives a curved but monotone relationship and is the safer default on ordinal data.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4], "b": [1, 4, 9, 16]})
print(round(df["a"].corr(df["b"]), 2), round(df["a"].corr(df["b"], method="spearman"), 2))

topics.title: qcut makes equal-count buckets
topics.body: `cut` splits by value ranges; `qcut` splits into groups of roughly equal size. Deciles of spend need qcut, because a fixed range would put almost everyone in one bucket.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
print(pd.qcut(s, 3).value_counts().sort_index().tolist())

topics.title: describe(include='all') covers text
topics.body: The default summary skips text. `include="all"` adds count, unique and top for the object columns, which is the difference between a numeric profile and a full one.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi"], "v": [1, 2]})
print(df.describe(include="all").shape[0])

interviewBank.q: Walk through your first fifteen minutes with an unknown dataset.
interviewBank.answer: Shape and dtypes, then missing counts and duplicates, then value counts for categories and `describe` for numerics, then a correlation look at the numeric columns. Each step decides the next question, and anything surprising becomes a note for the report.

interviewBank.q: How do you avoid reporting a correlation that is really a group effect?
interviewBank.answer: Check the relationship inside each segment as well as overall. Simpson's paradox is exactly this: a positive overall trend can reverse inside every group when the groups differ in size and level.

interviewBank.q: How do you turn an EDA observation into a finding?
interviewBank.answer: Name the segment, give the metric with its denominator, and state what would falsify it. "Pune learners pass at 62% of 812 attempts" is a finding; "Pune looks better" is an impression.

interviewBank.q: What is Simpson's paradox in a Pandas table?
interviewBank.answer: An overall trend that reverses inside every segment, because the segments differ in size and baseline. Group by the segment and compare the relationship within groups before reporting the pooled number.

defenseBank.q: Defend reporting a median and a p95 instead of a mean.
defenseBank.answer: The mean is pulled by the tail and answers "total divided by count", which no user experiences. The median describes the typical case and p95 describes the worst case that still matters, which is what a decision usually needs.

defenseBank.q: A stakeholder asks for "the average engagement". What do you clarify first?
defenseBank.answer: The grain and the denominator: average per user, per session or per day, and whether a user with no activity counts as zero. Those three choices can change the number by an order of magnitude.

interview.q: Walk through your first fifteen minutes with an unknown dataset.
interview.answer: Shape and dtypes, then missing counts and duplicates, then value counts for categories and `describe` for numerics, then a correlation look at the numeric columns. Each step decides the next question, and anything surprising becomes a note for the report.

interview.q: How do you avoid reporting a correlation that is really a group effect?
interview.answer: Check the relationship inside each segment as well as overall. Simpson's paradox is exactly this: a positive overall trend can reverse inside every group when the groups differ in size and level.

interview.q: How do you turn an EDA observation into a finding?
interview.answer: Name the segment, give the metric with its denominator, and state what would falsify it. "Pune learners pass at 62% of 812 attempts" is a finding; "Pune looks better" is an impression.

interview.q: What is Simpson's paradox in a Pandas table?
interview.answer: An overall trend that reverses inside every segment, because the segments differ in size and baseline. Group by the segment and compare the relationship within groups before reporting the pooled number.

defense.q: Defend reporting a median and a p95 instead of a mean.
defense.answer: The mean is pulled by the tail and answers "total divided by count", which no user experiences. The median describes the typical case and p95 describes the worst case that still matters, which is what a decision usually needs.

defense.q: A stakeholder asks for "the average engagement". What do you clarify first?
defense.answer: The grain and the denominator: average per user, per session or per day, and whether a user with no activity counts as zero. Those three choices can change the number by an order of magnitude.

interviewBank.q: Where does Pandas actually get slow?
interviewBank.answer: Row-wise Python work: `iterrows`, `apply(axis=1)` and per-group Python functions. Column operations run in compiled code, so the wins come from rewriting a row loop as column arithmetic or a groupby aggregation.

interviewBank.q: When should you stop using Pandas?
interviewBank.answer: When the working set no longer fits comfortably in memory, or when a single machine cannot finish in the time budget. Then move to chunked processing for a one-off, or to a query engine, Parquet plus DuckDB, or a distributed tool when it is recurring.

interviewBank.q: What is the first performance change you try on a slow Pandas pipeline?
interviewBank.answer: Find the row-wise step: `iterrows` or `apply(axis=1)` is usually where the time goes. Rewrite it as column arithmetic or a groupby transform, then measure again rather than assuming.

interviewBank.q: Why is a naive `int8` downcast risky?
interviewBank.answer: The cast does not raise on overflow; it wraps to a negative number. Check min and max against the dtype's range before casting, or use a nullable type and a validation step.

defenseBank.q: Defend measuring before optimising a dataframe pipeline.
defenseBank.answer: Memory and time are dominated by one or two columns or steps. `memory_usage(deep=True)` and a timed section show which, and optimising anything else risks complicating code for no measurable gain.

defenseBank.q: A 4 GB CSV must be summarised on a 8 GB laptop. Outline the approach.
defenseBank.answer: Read in chunks and aggregate each chunk into a small result, or convert once to Parquet and read only the needed columns. Either way the peak is a chunk plus the summary, not the file plus a copy.

topics.title: to_numpy hands over the values
topics.body: `to_numpy()` drops the index and returns one dtype array, which is what scikit-learn expects. Check the dtype: mixed columns become object.

print(arr.shape, arr.dtype)

topics.title: A DataFrame from an array needs names
topics.body: An array has no column names, so the frame supplies them. Without the names, every later selection is positional and fragile.
topics.code:

import numpy as np

arr = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
df = pd.DataFrame(arr, columns=["a", "b"])
print(df.columns.tolist())

topics.title: SQL and Pandas say the same thing
topics.body: SELECT is column selection, WHERE is a mask, GROUP BY is groupby, JOIN is merge. Knowing the mapping is how a query becomes a frame and back.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
out = df[df["sales"] > 5].groupby("city")["sales"].sum()
print(out.to_dict())

topics.title: Split before you compute statistics
topics.body: Fit any statistic on the training rows and apply it to the test rows. Computing the mean over the full table leaks test information into training.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3, 100]})
train = df.iloc[:3]
test = df.iloc[3:]
mean = train["x"].mean()
print(mean, round(float((test["x"] - mean).abs().iloc[0]), 1))

topics.title: Encode categories for a model
topics.body: One-hot encoding is the safe default for a nominal category; an integer code implies an order the model will use.

topics.title: Series.to_numpy copies by default
topics.body: `to_numpy()` may share memory for a single dtype, and `copy=True` makes the boundary explicit. Knowing which you got matters when a model or a library writes into the array.

import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 2])
arr = s.to_numpy(copy=True)

print(s.tolist())

interviewBank.q: What is data leakage, in one concrete Pandas example?
interviewBank.answer: Filling missing values or scaling with a statistic computed on the full dataset before splitting. The test rows influenced the transformation, so the validation score is optimistic and does not survive production.

interviewBank.q: Why does scikit-learn prefer a NumPy array while analysis prefers a DataFrame?
interviewBank.answer: The estimator needs a numeric matrix with no labels and no mixed dtypes, so an array is the unambiguous input. Analysis needs names, alignment and mixed types, which the frame provides; `to_numpy` is the boundary.

interviewBank.q: Where exactly is the DataFrame/Numpy boundary in a model pipeline?
interviewBank.answer: After all row-level work — filtering, joining, encoding, splitting — and before the estimator. `to_numpy(dtype=float)` at that point gives the model an unambiguous numeric matrix, while the frame keeps the labels for reporting.

interviewBank.q: How do you explain data leakage to a non-specialist?
interviewBank.answer: It is marking your own homework: the preparation step was allowed to look at the answers it will be tested on. The score looks excellent and then collapses in production, because the information it relied on will not be there.

defenseBank.q: Defend one-hot encoding over integer codes for city.
defenseBank.answer: City is nominal: an integer code tells the model Pune is between Delhi and Mumbai, which is false. One-hot removes the invented order at the cost of more columns, which is manageable for a small vocabulary.
steps: Name the cost of the fix.

defenseBank.q: A pipeline scores 0.98 in validation and 0.6 in production. Give your first hypothesis.
defenseBank.answer: Leakage: a feature or a transformation saw information it will not have in production, usually statistics computed before the split or a column derived from the target. Verify by rebuilding the split first, then the transforms inside it.

defense.q: Defend one-hot encoding over integer codes for city.
defense.answer: City is nominal: an integer code tells the model Pune is between Delhi and Mumbai, which is false. One-hot removes the invented order at the cost of more columns, which is manageable for a small vocabulary.
steps: Name the cost of the fix.

defense.q: A pipeline scores 0.98 in validation and 0.6 in production. Give your first hypothesis.
defense.answer: Leakage: a feature or a transformation saw information it will not have in production, usually statistics computed before the split or a column derived from the target. Verify by rebuilding the split first, then the transforms inside it.

modules.title: Professional Projects and Career
modules.goal: Run one analysis end to end, defend every choice, and present it as portfolio work.

topics.title: An analysis is a pipeline, not a script
topics.body: Load, validate, clean, analyse, report. Naming the stages makes each one testable and lets a reviewer see where a number came from.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 2], "marks": [80, None, 90]})
clean = raw.drop_duplicates("id").fillna({"marks": raw["marks"].median()})
print(clean.shape[0], clean["marks"].mean())

topics.title: State the grain before any number
topics.body: One row per what? Answering that decides whether a total is a sum, a mean or a count of distinct ids.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"user": [1, 1, 2], "minutes": [10, 20, 30]})
print(df["minutes"].sum())
print(df.groupby("user")["minutes"].sum().mean())

topics.title: A finding needs a denominator
topics.body: "40% of learners" means nothing without the base. Print the count next to every rate so the reader can judge it.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"passed": [True, False, False, True]})
print(df["passed"].sum(), len(df), round(df["passed"].mean() * 100, 1))

topics.title: Write the report the stakeholder asked for
topics.body: A table with the metric, the segment and the count is more useful than a plot with no labels. Build that table first, then chart it.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "passed": [True, False, True]})
report = df.groupby("city")["passed"].agg(learners="size", pass_rate="mean").round(2)
print(report.to_dict("index"))

topics.title: Reproducibility is a feature
topics.body: A seed, a pinned dtype map and a saved intermediate table let someone else rerun the analysis and get the same number.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.DataFrame({"x": range(6)})
seed = 7
sample = raw.sample(3, random_state=seed)["x"].tolist()
print(sample == raw.sample(3, random_state=seed)["x"].tolist())

topics.title: Write the question before the query
topics.body: A written question names the grain, the metric and the comparison. Without it, a table can be technically correct and still not answer what was asked.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"user": [1, 1, 2], "minutes": [10, 20, 30]})
print("per user:", df.groupby("user")["minutes"].sum().mean())
print("per attempt:", df["minutes"].mean())

topics.title: A cleaning log is part of the deliverable
topics.body: Recording what was dropped and why is what makes a number reviewable. A log line is a count, a rule and a reason.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1, 2], "v": [1, 2, 3]})
clean = raw.drop_duplicates("id", keep="last")
print(len(raw), len(clean))

topics.title: Reproducible means rerunnable
topics.body: A stored seed and a fixed input make the same output tomorrow. Anything without one is a screenshot, not an analysis.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": range(6)})
a = df.sample(3, random_state=11)["x"].tolist()
b = df.sample(3, random_state=11)["x"].tolist()
print(a == b)

topics.title: Present the table, then the chart
topics.body: A stakeholder needs the number they can quote and the picture that explains it. Shipping only one of the two forces them to recompute or to trust blindly.
topics.code:

interviewBank.q: Walk an interviewer through a Pandas project in four sentences.
interviewBank.answer: The question and the grain, the data and its quality problems, the transformations and why each was chosen, then the finding with its denominator and the check that would falsify it. Four sentences prove you can hold the whole pipeline.

interviewBank.q: How do you answer "what was the hardest bug"?
interviewBank.answer: Name a bug with a cause, not a symptom: a merge that fanned out because the key was not unique, found by comparing row counts, fixed with `validate` and a dedupe. The lesson is the check, not the fix.

interviewBank.q: How do you present one finding in 30 seconds?
interviewBank.answer: Question, method in one clause, the number with its denominator, and the decision it supports. Stop there; the notebook is the backup, not the pitch.

interviewBank.q: What is the most common mistake in a junior Pandas project?
interviewBank.answer: Trusting a row count — counting attempts as users, or a fan-out join that silently multiplied rows. Checking grain and counts before every aggregate catches most of it.

defenseBank.q: Defend including a cleaning notebook in your portfolio.
defenseBank.answer: It shows the judgement employers test: what was wrong with the data, which rows were removed and why, and what the numbers looked like before and after. A model with no cleaning trail cannot be audited.

defenseBank.q: Your manager asks for one chart. What do you deliver instead, and why?
defenseBank.answer: The chart plus the table it came from and the two-line finding. The table lets them check the number and reuse it; the finding states what the chart means, which is the part they actually asked for.
